title: Satisfaction
hookLine: Anselm pictured the cross as Christ restoring God's honor on our behalf

lines: A WORLD OF LORDS AND OATHS.
cards: "Forgive us our debts." That's how the Lord's Prayer reads in Matthew's Gospel, in the old King James words. Not mistakes.
Not trespasses. Debts. As if every wrong leaves an unpaid bill behind it.

Anselm, the archbishop who asked why God became human, took that picture seriously. Some historians link his thinking to a world of lords and oaths, where honor was owed, and a broken promise had to be made good.
His question was hard and clear: if sin is a debt to God, what does it take to settle it? Yesterday's picture was a battlefield. Today's is a ledger.

teach.b: Forget the modern meaning, the feeling after a good meal. In Anselm's picture, satisfaction means making amends: doing what's needed to put a wrong right. He lays it out in his dialogue Why God Became Human.
Every creature owes God honor: its whole life and will, turned toward God. Sin is holding that back. And here's the trap.
Even if you lived perfectly from tomorrow on, you'd only be paying what you already owed for tomorrow. Nothing is left over to cover yesterday. So the debt stands.
Anselm says a wrong against honor can end only two ways: it's made good, or it's punished. God, he says, chooses to make it good. Not a penalty, but a repair.
On day one thousand eighty we heard who Anselm thought could do that: only one who is both God and human.
Christ's freely given life, which he never owed to death, is a gift so great it more than covers what humanity held back.
Paul has his own picture of a bill wiped out: "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross."
Not every church tells the story with Anselm's ledger, and those who do build on it in different ways. Notice what it is not.
In Anselm's telling, the cross isn't punishment. It's payment. That difference comes back tomorrow.

how: Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's wording ask God to forgive their debts, and in some churches the language of Christ paying what humanity owed is heard in hymns, sermons and the prayers at communion.

o: a punishment that pays back a crime
the full feeling after a good meal
making amends to put a wrong right

p: the handwriting nailed to the cross

s: in Anselm's picture, the cross is a punishment
Anselm says a wrong is either made good or punished. God chooses to make it good: payment, not punishment.
Matthew's Lord's Prayer in the King James asks God to forgive our debts
"forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
Anselm thought good behavior from now on could pay for the past
you'd only be paying what you already owed for the future. nothing is left over for yesterday.

games.q: you're Anselm. honor owed to God has been held back. how can the wrong end?
o: God simply lets it go, as if it never happened.
it must be either made good or punished, and God chooses to make it good.
humans try harder until the debt is cleared.
games.why: Anselm says it's satisfaction or punishment. God chooses satisfaction, and only someone both human and divine can pay it.

practice: Think of a debt someone paid for you; it doesn't have to be money: someone covered for you, made good on a promise you broke, stayed up so you could sleep. Notice the size of it, and that you couldn't have paid it yourself.
If you pray, hold that picture next to the cross and say thank you; if you don't, just stay with the person who paid.

wordCard.voice: Satisfaction. In Anselm's picture, making amends for a wrong against God's honor: a debt humans owe and only the God-man can pay.

orig.note: Latin: Anselm's word for making amends, putting a wrong right.

carryVoice: Your line: he paid what we owed. A gift bigger than the bill. Go gently.
